If you like old school point-and-click adventure games, then you might also enjoy this one. If you don't like them, then it's very unlikely that this game would be your exception.

Personally, I love them, and this game exemplifies a lot of what I enjoy about the genre. There's a large quantity of extremely necessary reading, as numerous clues are hidden in notes, journals, scientific reports, etc. The journal entries and scientific reports are particularly well-written imo, and I really liked delving into them and teasing out the plot-relevant details. Puzzles are logical and suited to the story, and the game plays fair with providing background info and hints...sometimes even more than once. There's one puzzle that you can solve in at least three different ways! The triggers for plot progression are mostly well-judged; there's only one that really bugged me, in which a location was off-limits for no discernible reason until the game decided it was time for me to explore there.

On the less positive side, the graphics are dated and the voice-acting is amateurish (though not the worst I've heard), neither of which bothers me overly much but which may turn some people off. Also, the first time I played the game I was able to complete it without any outside help, but the second time I was playing with a darker monitor, and I ended up relying on a let's play to find some objects that I [i]knew[/i] were there but couldn't locate in the shadows. This problem was exacerbated by the navigational controls, which are a bit on the clunky side.

The atmosphere is more unsettling than it is scary. There are a couple of very minor jump scares (seriously, so minor they barely qualify). Some of the sound effects are wonderfully subtle and eerie, however, and provide a nice sense of dread in certain scenes.

And a couple of pieces of advice if you decide to play the game: 1) Keep pen and paper handy when you play. You don't have an in-game journal, and there's a lot of info you'll need to keep track of. 2) This isn't readily obvious when you're playing, but there are two possible endings, one good and one bad. Take care to get the one you want!

I have mixed feelings about this game. My expectations aren't excessive for a title that costs less than a tenner, but when it's a bit dissatisfying in the end, does that cheap price somehow balance it out?

The video it shows is a bit misleading, since it appears to be slightly rough 3d but is in fact static pre-rendered scenes that you flick to in a slightly awkward fashion. That panning camera shot is not even in the game, and generally nothing moves in a frame bar some jump-scares or the effect for a flash-light.

I can ignore the amateurish production values on the voice-work and the performances, but it's clunky to play. With it easy to miss things of importance due to how you "move" around the world. Think of it like "google maps: the game" as it jerks forward and then you wave your mouse pointer around to see if there's any response.

Repeat that gingerly in every direction to see if there's anything at all of relevance around you, and then move on. Initially I found the mental challenges to be quite pleasant and logical, but as it went on it became increasingly tedious trying to spot fiddly "sweet-spots" of interactivity.

Then you have the odd contradictory puzzle that doesn't follow the same rules, or is a bit silly. Not in the sense of the solution being ridiculous or nonsensical, but still a bit "red herring-like". An example of this: someone hides an item and then programs a GPS so they can locate it later. 

Yet the GPS only works in one spot, which is about ten feet from where you initially find it and right in front of your face. This item is hidden under a fire-extinguisher, yet I walked around the entire area thinking it would be buried in the ground or some-such. 

I know that that is my own fault, yet it's annoying to have "puzzles" where the clues suggest a more complicated solution and you traipse around futilely looking for something that isn't even that well-hidden. Most of the puzzles are quite good to solve, with detective work and mental reasoning  being the driving factor, but stuff like that feels like a misstep to me.

SPOILERS!!!!!!!

Beyond that, the story is.....uh....well, crap. It suggests a great evil awakening and something monstrous being unleashed, but it's pretty comical when you find out what is actually terrorising this quaint location. I get that this is based on British myths, and some people will find that fascinating, yet I was expecting a terrible demon, or whatnot, and instead got....a killer rock.  

Now, I am British and I am aware of our myths, but nonetheless....It's incredibly daft to see it happening, even if there's a load of superstition about it. To my tastes it wasn't a great reveal, and when I add in the irritating format and (the few) puzzles that didn't quite hit the mark, I can't recommend it overall.

Barrow Hill is a short, moody point-and-click adventure that delivers exactly what it promises: mysterious ruins, creeping dread, and plenty of strange symbols to poke at under dim flashlight beams. If you grew up on Myst or The Lost Crown, you will feel right at home here.

The game runs at a fixed 800×600 resolution (which I only noticed after wrestling with it for a long while in DXWND). Despite that, once I got it windowed properly, the experience was smooth and immersive. It is much easier to see and play if you just let it hijack your resolution for the duration, though. There are not any volume-adjustment options, and the game is very loud, I had to remember to turn my speakers down by like 60% before starting the game.

The puzzles are intuitive for the most part. At around 10 hours long (including my really messing-up at the end and having to go backwards to go forwards...), it is a tight, dark, eerie adventure. It may be short, but it earns its place as a cult classic. Just know going in: this game is a product of its time—and that is part of the charm.

Final thoughts: spooky, simple, satisfying. Just do not expect modern resolution—or to ever figure out what the paintbrush is for...

Barrow Hill is missing something, in a broad sense. Maybe it's the unskippable radio programs; maybe it's the unskippable phone calls; maybe it's the unskippable 12 (or more) times you have to listen to someone ominously reciting two sentences. Maybe it's the way the written materials are almost entirely about the plot at hand - to the point that near the end of the game, when you unlock an entire new area long since abandoned and left to rot, you get absolutely no context on why it was abandoned at all. Maybe it's the little quality-of-life moments, like doors having to be unlocked each time you approach them or not being able to move while on the phone. Maybe it's just my personal issue with the nitty gritty of the plot.

I understand and respect that this was essentially one person's passion project, so I really don't mean to sound harsh. That new area I mentioned above has a great atmosphere, and there are some musical stings that really stabbed me with dread at times. I wouldn't say the voice acting was as poor as others call it. The opening and closing cutscenes being real-life (low-res) video was quaint and, speaking specifically of the opening, set a great tone before I really started playing. And there are some moments where you can skip to the end of a puzzle without having triggered it by viewing or doing something else, which I always appreciate. (I usually will use a walkthrough for these kinds of adventure games that leave you on your own, so it's nice to be able to cheat a puzzle.)

But again, something is missing. I'm a sucker for historical mysteries, weird supernatural occurrences, and the unearthing of ruins, but this plot held no fascination for me at all. I wasn't invested in the characters we meet, I wasn't afraid of the entity/ies potentially on the prowl, and by my 8th time hearing "THE ANCIENT. MAN. HAS AWOKEN." I was downright over it.

Someone elsewhere in the reviews compared this to Rhiannon: Curse of the Four Branches, and I will say that I was independently reminded of that game as well when playing, particularly when completing the last extended puzzle sequence. In my view, Rhiannon does a lot right that Barrow Hill does wrong. It can be clunky and occasionally cheesy, but it absolutely nails an atmosphere that Barrow Hill (despite being set in a creepy forest at night, for crying out loud) somehow misses, and presents captivating lore through a set of varying written materials and recordings. Thinking of Barrow Hill's written logs vs Rhiannon's, I find myself hard-pressed to really distinguish any traits of the former's characters via their writing, and that's a fatal error for a game so intent on telling its story that way. (To put it differently, they seemed to exist to tell the story of the game, not to be real people who found themselves plopped into a horror movie setting.)

If the developer is ever inclined, I think Barrow Hill deserves a remake. The graphics and voice acting need not be perfect, but some rewriting, reworking of mechanics such as the phone calls, and a shakedown of the controls for easier freedom of movement would work wonders. It's got a solid something at its core that needs to be polished up a bit. But as it stands, I was actively rushing through to say I'd finished it, which is not a great feeling.

I bought Barrow Hill out of nostalgia having originally played it in the mid 2000s. However, revisiting it reminded me of all the frustrating things about the game that I'd somehow repressed. First, the game can be incredibly glitchy at times with movement arrows not appearing or having to severely offset the cursor to perform an action. And speaking of movement, it's very counter-intuitive at times. Other games that require you to click at the screen edges aren't nearly so finicky. Also, while I don't need to be hand held in a game, there definitely needs to be some kind of direction which other point-and-click adventures do a better job at handling while still leaving it up to you to explore and puzzle solve. Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game to a new player and would caution any nostalgic replayers to take the rose-colored glasses off and think if this game is really worth the hassle. And if you do decide to purchase it and give it a go, just be aware that this game is tedious and frustrating, even by mid 2000s point-and-click standards.

Let me preface this review by stating that I think it has a lot of love put into it. It's very spooky not in the jumpscare manner that a lot of more modern horror games try to implement, but it's ambience and setting make you very nervous about what could be around the corner or down the unlit pathway you inevitably have to travel down. 
What puzzles I did end up solving were not so laughably easy that a toddler could do it but also not so frustrating that when the answer is found you don't end up throwing your arms up in the air and say "oh, come on, how was I supposed to know that?!".

That being said, the game has certain scripted events that one has to experience to even progress through the game, and frankly I had seen every screen I could reach at that point in the game well over five times and nothing new was there for me to do because I hadn't found what specific thing it wanted from me.
It feels like the kind of game that you need a guide for, which doesn't pair well with the fact that since it was made in 2006 - and isn't well known as far as I can tell - so one literally could not have had a guide when it was released. Instead, they had to beat their head against the metaphorical brick wall until either it broke or they did.
Which frankly, is a shame, because I really think this game should have gotten more attention and love back then and now.

As one of my original entries into the world of horror themed point and clicks back in the mid-2000s, Barrow Hill holds a very special place in my heart. This is a horror adventure that has a very kooky monster and one that I often tell my friends about. As one of Matt Clark's first advances into game making, it certainly has its flaws. The monster isn't overly scary, and there is some tedium with voice-lines that repeat over and over. (So much so that I still remember them to this day). But the idea, the story, that is sitting in this game has potential that is only held back by the chosen enemy, and perhaps some technical execution

Despite all that, the game is easy to play, and has very strong atmosphere that makes you feel isolated and alone on the Barrow. And if you happen to not spawn the monster within the first 20 mins of the game, there is some honest intrigue about what is happening. I think this early reveal is the biggest flaw of the game, and ruins a lot of what could be built up by the rest of it, along with its abysmal 2 hour playtime if you know what to do. This and exactly what the monster is, and what drives its actions is also a bit of a mystery and isn't well explored even by the explanations littered around the game. (It has everything to do with its chosen vessel.) 

So why, despite this do I recommend this game? Well, 1 is to support a long-standing developer who has good ideas mixed with celtic myth and 2, its a classic adventure game that, if you enjoy some silliness in like I do, will scratch that itch.

Creo que hay que estar muy mentalizado para elegir este juego. Hay que saber exactamente lo que te vas a encontrar para evitar decepciones. Barrow Hill: Curse of the Ancient Circle es una aventura gráfica a la antigua, complicada, con un personaje estático que no puede moverse con libertad usando las típicas teclas de dirección, es decir, que para girar o desplazarse hay que pinchar en el escenario. Esto implica que los objetos no resaltan ni se ven con facilidad y que no siempre son útiles, a veces están solo para decorar en medio de la profunda oscuridad. Además, los eventos importantes se consiguen a base de anotar muchas combinaciones de números y de escuchar audios y así todo. Si el jugador conoce estas características y decide seguir adelante estupendo, pero los que aborrezcan lo que he descrito ya pueden ir bajándose del vagón, porque no les va a gustar.

Sobre la historia del juego, cabe mencionar una fuerte influencia de las leyendas celtas (en concreto las que tienen que ver con los druidas). El terror no es abundante, se sugiere más que se muestra, pero el suspense sí que está presente a lo largo de toda la aventura. Hay muy pocos personajes con los que podemos interactuar y no son de gran ayuda precisamente porque han quedado algo tocados con la experiencia. El entorno, no obstante, es el punto fuerte de Barrow Hill; los bosques tenebrosos, las cafeterías abandonadas, las habitaciones sin huéspedes, las ruinas milenarias y las carreteras solitarias activarán nuestros sentidos poniéndonos alerta. El precio del producto no es caro, ya que el reto de pasárselo puede durar entre 2 y 5 horas para los que tengan una mente ágil y entiendan el inglés a la perfección, pero yo aconsejo comprarlo aunque sea con un poco de rebaja.

По сюжету мы оказываемся проездом в окрестностях реального графства Корнуолл, Англия. К несчастью, наша машина глохнет рядом с небольшим поселком Барроу-Хилл. Тут недавно были археологические раскопки, которые повлекли за собой цепь страшных событий, в которых нам предстоит разобраться. Мы не можем покинуть это место, а значит нам придется отправиться вглубь Барроу-Хилл и попытаться разрешить эту ситуацию.

Это классический для того времени Point & Click квест, где мы будем передвигаться путем щелкания направлений на экране. Поначалу привыкнуть будет сложно, но через пару часиков все будет в порядке. Несмотря на небольшой хронометраж в 5 часов игра сделана качественно и грамотно. Я бы вам не рекомендовал пытаться играть в умников-гигачадов и проходить все вслепую, ибо это и есть ловушка игры. Конечно все головоломки тут более чем логичные, но дело не в этом. В игре огромное количество предметов с которыми можно взаимодействовать. Календарик с котиком, куча мусора, печенька, нерешенный кроссворд и т.д. Что из этого поможет в прохождении вам будет абсолютно непонятно и если вам дорого ваше время, то я бы все-таки рекомендовал изредка подглядывать в гайд, как это делал я. Для общего представления о том, куда вы вообще идете.

Но у этой интерактивности есть и свои плюсы. Так как локации игры сделаны на основе реально существующих мест в графстве Корнуолл, тот тут можно почитать много всяких интересностей касательно быта англичан и посмотреть чем они увлекаются. Здесь очень много интерактивных объектов, которые можно потрогать и большое количество газетных статей и книг, где есть много интересных фактов и забавных подробностей. Любопытное зрелище.

Ну и конечно же плюс в карму разработчиков, за ностальгию по старому дизайну сайтов и интерфейсу Windows XP. Я как-будто снова попал в 2005, где подключение к интернету выдавало целый симфонический концерт из пикающих и скрипучих звуков, а сайты в интернете были цветастыми и кринжовыми.

Игра полностью на английском, но на просторах интернета есть русификатор с полной озвучкой и переводом. Касаемо головоломок, тут игре прям мое почтение. Некоторые вещи заставили меня конкретно задуматься, а их решение неожиданно оказалось более чем логичным. Также хочу похвалить местный эмбиент. Ночной шум леса записан прекрасно, а всякие поскрипывания, вздохи и прочие неприятные звуки действительно создают ощущение дискомфорта. Также тут есть рандомная генерация паролей и энкаунтеры в виде неожиданных звонков и местных обитателей. Я его не встречал, но, как поговаривают, в игре есть редкий энкаунтер, когда у нас за спиной в любой момент может оказаться противник, который вполне может нас убить. Главное не паниковать и стараться медленно отползти на противоположный от него экран. Вот бы самому встретить такую штуку.

Первая часть Barrow Hill оставила после себя приятные впечатления. Несмотря на неудобное управление и неочевидные головоломки, играть в это было интересно и я хорошо провел время. Единственное я немного не понял концовки, но видеоряд там зачетный. Это мрачный, атмосферный и качественный квест старой школы, который и по сей день может увлечь случайного игрока, который увлекается играми подобного жанра.

I rate Barrow Hill: Curse of the Ancient Circle 1.5/5. Overall, this first-person perspective mystery game is pretty bad. To make matters worse, Barrow Hill’s graphics were fairly out of date when it came out in 2006 and have aged badly since that time. Mediocre voice acting, no subtitles, several obtuse puzzles, a lack of replay value, a laughable monster and disappointing endings (both of this game’s 2 endings are disappointing) do not help matters. Ultimately, the only really good thing about Barrow Hill is how similar it feels to other, earlier, better mystery games (specifically Jonathan Boakes’ Dark Fall: The Journal and Dark Fall II: Lights Out, which is not surprising considering how much influence Jonathan Boakes had on Barrow Hill).

+ This is an extremely quiet, peaceful mystery game with a slow, creeping, brooding atmosphere ([spoiler]Until this carefully crafted atmosphere is largely ruined when you find out that the “monster” hunting you is essentially a giant, magical slab of rock[/spoiler]. The atmosphere really is well crafted though and there are many locations in this game which really do seem creepy in the classic Jonathan Boakes Dark Fall style. A quiet, creepy, brooding game can be nice once in a while, especially if you are more used to louder action-oriented games like I am.

+ This game has 2 jumpscares and one of them is fairly effective. 

+/- Barrow Hill has a classic mid-to-late 90s mystery game feel. It controls just like a first-person mystery game of that time (and it looks just like one too). The graphics are subdued and brooding mostly still images (this game has very little animation of any kind). Remember the environments in the original early Resident Evil games? The images which comprise this game’s environments have that same sort of quality. Controlling the game is done entirely with the mouse. Changing your location or turning the direction you are pointing is accomplished by clicking near the edges of the screen. Zooming in on objects is accomplished by clicking when the cursor becomes an hourglass, etc. The controls work but are also clunky and limited though these rudimentary controls are responsive.

+/- Barrow Hill has almost no music (other than music heard over the in-game radios found in certain locations) though there are some very creepy ambient sounds which set the mood nicely.

+/- This game takes some time to complete even with the use of a walkthrough guide. I recommend playing the game yourself (if you want to waste your time by playing this game) and see how far you can get and then, once you get stuck, begin using a walkthrough to get through the more obtuse, less logical or more irritating puzzles. Doing this will dramatically reduce the frustration of playing this game. The guide I used is Barrow Hill Guide by Rainbowheart02. The puzzles, in general, are not nearly as good or as purely logical as those found in the first 2 Dark Fall games and some environments seem to go largely unused. 

+/- You mean I have to actually READ stuff?! Barrow Hill has a lot of stuff to read (fliers, pamphlets, newspaper clippings, etc. and it fully expects that you should actually read it all. It is generally interesting stuff to read but hey, reading Wikipedia is fun too and that’s a lot more informative than playing this stupid game. 

- Barrow Hill: The Curse of the Magic Circle has a really stupid sounding title. This game sounds like some sort of Nancy Drew/Hardy Boys children’s mystery story and I doubt that you will be taken seriously ever again if you spend more than 8 hours playing this (as I have).

- This game REQUIRES you to be able to WRITE NOTES BY HAND. This is a CRAZY design choice. Barrow Hill has the completely UNREALISTIC expectation, and NON-USER-FRIENDLY concept that in order to complete this game you, a videogame player, should be forced to somehow TAKE NOTES. This game requires you to write down door code combinations, a phone number, a license plate number and even, do AN ACTUAL CALCULATION of 4 x 68578 (or something like that), on a calculator which you have to go find somehow IN THE REAL WORLD. Ugh. I’m not sure if it was worth it. Why can’t this game just do this kind of stuff for you?

- There is no way to rebind controls (though I never felt a need to do so). You cannot even change the mouse sensitivity though this was never a problem for me.

- There is no way to change volume levels inside the game.

- There are no subtitles and all the characters have various fairly thick English accents. They spoke clearly enough for me to understand though (barely).

- The extremely jerky animations which display when a character is speaking look like 2 frames repeating over and over again and look preposterous.

- The voice acting isn’t that great anyhow. The characters sound terrified in the manner that someone would be terrified to get a parking ticket.

- There is a link to the developer’s website on the game’s main menu. If you click it though it takes you to a now defunct website and freezes up the game. Every time you exit the game anyhow though, the game takes a few minutes to actually close before you can re-enter it.

- There is no way to adjust the game’s resolution so on a now standard 1080p resolution screen, all the game’s graphics are a bit stretched out. I got the feeling that this game was intended to be run at 800 by 600 pixels which, even in 2006, was a bit low.

- There are no steam achievements, no backgrounds, no emoticons, no etc.

- There are 2 endings, both of which are accessible towards the very end of the game and neither of which is very satisfying. The reasons for exactly why one ending is supposedly better than the other are left cryptic and mysterious. [spoiler] One (the easier ending) is fairly unexplained and shows jerky images of a construction crane and a subway entrance for unknown reasons and then nothing. I guess that’s the ‘bad’ ending because someone apparently hates cranes and subway entrances. The other, harder ending has a somewhat vague, somber epilogue which only cryptically explains exactly what the game was all about. The overall, environmentalist message is about trying to maintain balance between nature and development in the environment. You never really learn what is really buried under the hill or who or what put it there. Anything specific related to this game’s plot is apparently lost to time. [/spoiler] Neither ending requires replaying the game (merely reloading an earlier save and solving 1 additional puzzle is all that’s necessary to get the harder of the 2 endings) nor is there any real point in replaying this game anyhow. Barrow Hill has little to no replay value.

- The monster hunting you in this game is [spoiler] just a giant slab of rock which (when you are not looking at it apparently) moves around and turns people to ash when it touches them. I am not kidding. At one point you even see it attacking people in some extremely jerky security camera footage. Upon seeing that, most tension this game wanted to create was GONE. How cheap can the production values of a mystery a game get? [/spoiler]

 While the aesthetics of the old cell phones, "video chats" and other graphic elements may look old they are not "yuck" now, but rather charming. This is thanks to the wonderful design choices made by the creator Matt Clark.
Speaking of, Matt Clark basically created this entire game. He still lives and works near where this game is set and still makes games! Incredible!

If you like the old-style point & click mysteries of Myst, Nancy Drew, and more this game is for you. A true hidden gem, and in my opinion, a classic.
